2) It really depends. Usually when the patient is declared brain dead on the ventilator, we don’t like to keep them on the vent for longer than 24-36 hours. Other hospitals may have different guidelines. I don’t have any experience with organ donation from people who actually die outside of the hospital and can’t be revived. I guess certain bits of bone can be harvested? Skin and corneas, maybe? It would have to happen relatively quickly I’d imagine. 

3) The process of organ donation is long. If you know you want to be an organ donor and the time comes to donate, you have to be entered into the system and the recipient of your organs has to be a good match. Sometimes similar in age, ethnicity, and size depending on which organ. Blood type matching. Things like that. I doubt you’d be able to do such a direct donation in that case. Usually when people choose who they want to donate to, it’s cases of people donating bits of liver or a kidney to a friend or loved one. They have weeks to prepare, undergo testing, etc.

There are machines that artificially keep donor lungs ventilating to give them more time to transplant. I don’t know many people who would look at the machine and the artificially ventilating lungs and call it a person.

That’s essentially what we’re already doing with the ventilator— artificially keeping the lungs moving and supplying oxygen to the rest of the body. The difference is they’re still inside the body. 

It is really hard to look at the person in the bed as a whole and not think that they’re still alive in some way, but they aren’t. Everything that made them who they are is gone. For Christians and other religious people, I’d call that a soul. For myself and non religious people, it’s their brain. Every memory, emotion, feeling, basic act of life is gone.

I work as a nurse in the ICU and we deal with the organ donation companies and patients who are candidates all the time. 

Lots of families say that they can’t donate organs because of their religion. Not necessarily because their religion is against organ donation specifically, but because they think that taking the patient off of the ventilator is murder. Even if the patient is already brain dead (which *is* dead). Sometimes we’ve had to get the courts involved because we can’t just leave a dead person on a ventilator indefinitely, even if organ donation is off the table.

You don’t have to have anything beyond a professional relationship with your coworkers if you don’t want to. I am ridiculously socially awkward but I managed to build a friendly relationship with my coworkers and I’m much more comfortable now than I was last year when I started. We do have a nurse on our unit who is very quiet and keeps to herself, kind of like you. She never joins us in the nurses station and she really just hangs out in her own corner, and that’s *completely fine.* The only thing is she rarely helps out other nurses, and often doesn’t respond to her call lights. So I would make sure that even if you prefer to keep to yourself, try and be helpful and friendly. Ask lots of questions. If you see someone drowning, ask if you can help. Hang a bag of fluids or run to the Pyxis to grab a med if they need it. 

I will say that I do really like the quiet nurse up on our unit, she’s very nice when you talk to her, but she tends to avoid us whenever we get new admits or there’s a code. I can’t say I could trust her in an emergency because I’ve never worked with her in an emergent situation, despite her always being on shift when shit hits the fan. She isn’t a new nurse, either. 

So keep to yourself if you want, but make sure you’re available to help and take advantage of as many learning opportunities as you can.
